cls: Active (reduced) folate / medical food (folate vitamer; e.g., Deplin, Metafolin)
pharm: Bioactive folate - one-carbon (methyl) donor and substrate for homocysteine remethylation and CNS monoamine (serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine) synthesis
quick: Depression adjunct (medical food): 7.5-15 mg orally once daily; folate deficiency / supplementation: 1 mg or per product (e.g., 1-7.5 mg) once daily
May be taken with or without food; once-daily dosing aids adherence
Folate is important in pregnancy; L-methylfolate is an accepted active folate form - use the indicated dose; do not exceed prescribed amounts without advice
Folate is normally present in milk and recommended in lactation; considered compatible at appropriate doses
No specific adjustment for ordinary doses; folate is water-soluble
No specific adjustment; L-methylfolate bypasses hepatic DHFR/MTHFR conversion
Chronic alcohol use impairs folate status; limit alcohol
Mood/depression response; exclude/treat vitamin B12 deficiency before high-dose folate; CBC if anemia
summary: L-Methylfolate (L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate, 5-MTHF) is the active, ready-to-use form of folate that circulates in plasma and crosses the blood-brain barrier - unlike folic acid, it does not require reduction by dihydrofolate reductase or methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR). It is the principal one-carbon (methyl) donor for the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine (regenerating S-adenosylmethionine) and is a cofactor in the synthesis of the monoamine neurotransmitters serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. It is marketed and regulated in the United States as a MEDICAL FOOD (e.g., Deplin) for the dietary management of suboptimal folate in patients with depression (often as an adjunct to antidepressants) and as an active folate supplement in folate deficiency, including in people with reduced MTHFR activity. IMPORTANT: it is a medical food / dietary supplement and is NOT an FDA-approved drug; the data and dosing come from medical-food labeling and the clinical literature rather than an FDA drug label. As with any folate, vitamin B12 deficiency should be excluded or treated first, because folate can mask the hematologic signs of B12 deficiency while neurologic damage progresses.
indications: Dietary management of suboptimal folate (L-methylfolate) status in patients with major depressive disorder, including as an adjunct to antidepressant therapy (medical food)
Dietary management of folate deficiency, including in patients with reduced MTHFR enzyme activity or impaired folate metabolism
Active folate supplementation when an already-reduced folate form is preferred over folic acid
Adjunctive folate provision in conditions associated with elevated homocysteine or increased folate needs (per labeling/clinical judgment)

dosage.d: 7.5-15 mg L-methylfolate once daily (15 mg commonly used as adjunct in MDD)
dosage.n: Used with or as an adjunct to antidepressants; medical-food labeling, not an FDA drug indication

dosage.d: 1 mg once daily (or per product, e.g., 1-7.5 mg)
dosage.n: Active 5-MTHF form; useful when MTHFR activity is reduced

dosage.c: Reduced MTHFR activity / folate metabolism support
dosage.d: Per product labeling (commonly 1-15 mg once daily depending on indication)
dosage.n: Bypasses the MTHFR conversion step needed for folic acid

admin: Take by mouth once daily, with or without food; swallow tablets/capsules whole
Before starting higher-dose folate, evaluate for and treat vitamin B12 deficiency to avoid masking it and allowing neurologic injury to progress
Continue antidepressant therapy when L-methylfolate is used as an adjunct for depression - it is added to, not a replacement for, prescribed treatment
Store and use per the product (medical-food) labeling; the dose differs between general supplementation (often ~1 mg) and depression adjunct use (7.5-15 mg)
Inform the clinician of all supplements; counsel that this is a medical food, not an FDA-approved prescription drug
moa: L-Methylfolate is the biologically active, already-reduced form of folate (L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate). Whereas folic acid and dietary folates must be reduced - by dihydrofolate reductase and then methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) - to become active, L-methylfolate is the end product of that pathway and is directly usable; this is clinically relevant in people with reduced MTHFR activity. It serves as the methyl donor that, together with vitamin B12-dependent methionine synthase, remethylates homocysteine to methionine, regenerating S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe), the universal methyl donor for numerous methylation reactions. In the central nervous system, adequate methylfolate (which crosses the blood-brain barrier) supports the synthesis of the monoamine neurotransmitters serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine; correcting suboptimal central folate is the proposed basis for its adjunctive benefit in depression. It also supports DNA synthesis and red-cell production (hence its role in folate-deficiency anemias).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to L-methylfolate or product components
relative: Untreated/undiagnosed vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency - treat B12 first, as folate can correct the anemia while permitting progression of B12-related neurologic damage
History of bipolar disorder (caution when used adjunctively for mood)
monitor: Vitamin B12 status before and during higher-dose folate use
Complete blood count if treating anemia

preg: Folate is essential in pregnancy (notably for neural-tube development), and L-methylfolate is an accepted active folate form used in prenatal supplementation, including for women with reduced MTHFR activity. Use the indicated dose; high adjunct doses (e.g., for depression) should be used under clinical guidance, and patients should not exceed the labeled amount without advice.
lact: Folate is normally secreted into breast milk and is recommended during lactation. L-methylfolate at appropriate supplemental doses is considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is needed for ordinary doses; folate is water-soluble and excess is renally excreted.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is needed; an advantage of L-methylfolate is that it does not require hepatic reduction (DHFR) or MTHFR conversion to become active.

moderate: Methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine and other folate antagonists / dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors (folate may reduce efficacy of antifolate therapy; conversely these reduce folate status - separate and individualize)
Antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, valproate, carbamazepine) - folate may lower antiepileptic levels and these drugs lower folate; monitor seizure control and folate status
minor: Capecitabine/5-fluorouracil (folate can enhance fluoropyrimidine toxicity - use caution)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use impairs folate absorption and status; limit alcohol intake.
interactions.diagnostics: Supplementation raises serum/red-cell folate levels; obtain baseline folate and vitamin B12 before high-dose use, since folate can normalize the blood count and mask B12 deficiency.

common: Occasional nausea, bloating, or abdominal discomfort
Insomnia or irritability (more often when used at higher adjunct doses)
serious: Masking of vitamin B12 deficiency, allowing progression of B12-related neurologic damage (a risk of any folate, especially at high doses)
rare: Reports of altered mood/activation (e.g., agitation) in susceptible individuals

monitoring: Vitamin B12 status before and during higher-dose folate use (to avoid masking deficiency)
Depressive symptoms and treatment response when used adjunctively
Complete blood count when treating folate-deficiency anemia
Seizure control in patients on antiepileptic drugs
counsel: This is a medical food / active form of folate (vitamin B9), not an FDA-approved prescription drug - tell your clinician you are taking it
Take one dose by mouth each day, with or without food
If it is being used for depression, keep taking your prescribed antidepressant too - this is added on, not a replacement
Make sure your vitamin B12 has been checked, because folate can hide a B12 problem
It may take several weeks to notice a mood benefit; tell your doctor if you feel more agitated or have trouble sleeping
pk: Hematologic/biochemical effect over days to weeks; mood benefit over several weeks when used adjunctively
Plasma 5-MTHF peaks roughly 1-3 hours after an oral dose
Folate body stores turn over slowly; circulating 5-MTHF has a relatively short plasma half-life with daily dosing maintaining levels
Once-daily dosing maintains active folate levels; body folate stores buffer day-to-day
Store at room temperature in a tightly closed container, protected from light and moisture, per product labeling
pearls: MEDICAL FOOD / dietary supplement - NOT an FDA-approved drug; data drawn from medical-food labeling (e.g., Deplin/Metafolin) and the clinical literature rather than an FDA drug label
It is the ACTIVE, already-reduced folate (5-MTHF) and crosses the blood-brain barrier - it bypasses DHFR and the MTHFR conversion step that folic acid requires (relevant in reduced MTHFR activity)
ALWAYS exclude/treat vitamin B12 deficiency before high-dose folate - folate can correct anemia while B12 neurologic damage progresses
Common depression-adjunct dose is 15 mg once daily added to an antidepressant; deficiency/supplement doses are much lower (often ~1 mg)
Watch for interactions with antifolates (methotrexate, trimethoprim) and antiepileptic drugs (mutual reduction in levels)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next day's dose, skip the missed dose and resume your once-daily schedule - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: L-methylfolate has a wide margin of safety; excess water-soluble folate is largely excreted in the urine and acute overdose is unlikely to cause serious toxicity, though gastrointestinal upset, sleep disturbance, or irritability may occur. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive. The main clinically important hazard of excessive/long-term high-dose folate is masking of vitamin B12 deficiency.
